en: The Sūtra on the Merit of Constructing Stūpas Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty (whose name means "Sunshine" in the language of Tang).
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven upon a seat of white jade, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, great bodhisattvas, and the sovereign lord of the gods and his immeasurable retinue.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King, Nārāyaṇa, Maheśvara, and the five Gandharva Kings, each accompanied by their retinues, came together to the place where the Buddha was, desiring to ask the Tathāgata about the method for constructing stūpas and the measure of the merit produced by such stūpas.

In the assembly was a bodhisattva named Avalokiteśvara; knowing his thoughts, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

Now these devas, gandharvas, and others have come here for this purpose: they wish to request from the Tathāgata the method for constructing a stūpa, as well as the measure of the merit produced by such a stūpa.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for their sake, to benefit all immeasurable sentient beings!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: “Good son!

If any among the present assembly of devas, or all sentient beings of future ages, should establish a stūpa in any place where none yet exists—be it of such lofty and wondrous form as to transcend the three realms, or even as small as an *āmra* fruit;
with its banner-pole reaching up to the Brahma-heaven, or even as small as a needle;

with its wheel-canopy covering the great trichiliocosm, or even as small as a jujube leaf—and within that stūpa enshrine any portion of the Tathāgata’s relics, whether hair, teeth, beard, or nails, down to even a single fragment;

Whether one deposits the entire Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata’s twelve divisions of scripture, down to a single four-line verse, that person’s merit will be like that of Brahmā; after their life ends, they shall be reborn in the Brahma-world.
When his life there has ended, he will be reborn in the Five Pure Abodes, no different from those other devas.
Son of good family!
Such matters as I have described are the causes and conditions for the merit of the proportions of that stūpa; you devas should practice and learn them!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As previously stated regarding the enshrining of the śarīra and the Dharma-treasury, I have already accepted and upheld them."
"I do not fully understand the meaning of the Tathāgata’s four-line verse; I only pray that you will analyze and explain it for me!
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; I declare this to be dependent origination."
"Because causes and conditions have ceased, it is extinguished; this is what I have taught.
'O son of good family!
The meaning of this verse is called the Buddha’s Dharma-body; you should transcribe it and place it within that stūpa.'"
Why is this? Because all causes and conditions, as well as the nature of the dharmas produced thereby, are empty and quiescent; for this reason, I call it the Dharma-body.
If there are sentient beings who understand the meaning of such causes and conditions, you should know that such persons have seen the Buddha.

At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, along with all those gods, the great assembly, the gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Merit of Constructing Stupas
